chest-pain-causes-and-when-to-get-help.name: Chest pain: causes and when to get help
chest-pain-causes-and-when-to-get-help.summary: Most chest pain does not come from the heart, but sudden pain that does not ease or spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says that in most cases chest pain is not caused by a heart problem.
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, or pain that spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back.
The NHS says a person with these symptoms should not drive themselves to A&E.
For sharp or stabbing chest pain that changes with breathing, swallowing, coughing or lying down, the NHS suggests an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.

body.heading: What causes chest pain?
body.body: The NHS says that in most cases chest pain is not caused by a heart problem. Common causes that do not involve the heart include heartburn or indigestion, a strained chest muscle, anxiety or panic, and chest infections such as pneumonia or pleurisy. Shingles can also cause chest pain, often with a skin rash. The main heart-related causes are angina, heart attack and pericarditis. Pericarditis is inflammation of the lining around the heart, and the NHS says it often follows a viral infection such as a cold or flu.

body.heading: How do angina and a heart attack differ?
body.body: Angina is chest pain that comes and goes because blood flow to the heart is reduced, and it is often triggered by physical effort or stress. Angina attacks usually last less than 10 minutes. The NHS says chest pain is the most common sign of a heart attack, but symptoms vary: the pain is often severe, though some people have only minor pain similar to indigestion. Other signs include pain spreading to the arms, jaw, neck or back, sweating, breathlessness and feeling or being sick, and some people have these without any chest pain. Unlike the pain of angina, the symptoms of a heart attack are not usually relieved by a nitrate tablet or spray. A heart attack has similar symptoms but is more serious and needs emergency treatment. NHS 111 Wales says angina is usually caused by coronary heart disease, in which narrowed or blocked arteries reduce the blood supply to the heart.

body.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, or pain that spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back. Chest pain that comes with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or breathlessness is in the same group. The NHS says a person with these symptoms should not drive themselves to A&E. For someone already diagnosed with angina, the NHS treats pain that does not settle after rest or after their usual angina medicine as an emergency that needs a 999 call.

body.heading: When should chest pain be checked the same day?
body.body: For sharp or stabbing chest pain that changes with breathing, swallowing, coughing or lying down, the NHS suggests an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111. The NHS also advises getting help from NHS 111 for angina that is getting worse, happening more often or coming on at rest.

body.heading: What happens at the GP or in hospital?
body.body: The NHS says a GP who thinks a person has angina will refer them to a specialist. Tests can include an electrocardiogram (ECG), blood tests, blood oxygen tests or scans. An ECG records the heart's electrical activity. An NHS emergency department leaflet says staff check for serious causes such as a heart attack, a blood clot in the lung and a collapsed lung. The same leaflets describe troponin blood tests, which may be repeated, together with a chest X-ray or an ECG. A normal first troponin result lowers the chance of a heart problem but does not rule it out.

body.heading: How are angina and a heart attack treated?
body.body: For a heart attack, the blood tests look for troponin, a protein released when heart muscle is damaged, and further tests can include an echocardiogram and a coronary angiogram, which shows where blood flow is blocked. A heart attack is treated in hospital, and options include medicines to clear blockages, angioplasty with a stent, and bypass surgery. The NHS says the aims of angina treatment are to relieve symptoms, prevent further attacks, and reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke. Medicines include GTN for attacks and beta blockers or calcium channel blockers to prevent them, and surgery may be recommended to improve blood flow to the heart. Lifestyle changes the NHS lists for angina include a balanced diet, cutting down on alcohol, stopping smoking and losing weight if overweight.

headache-types-causes-and-warning-signs.name: Headaches: types, causes and warning signs
headache-types-causes-and-warning-signs.summary: Most headaches are tension-type headaches or migraines, but a sudden, extremely painful headache needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: NHS inform describes tension-type headache as the most common kind.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that comes on suddenly and is extremely painful, or one that follows a serious head injury.

NHS inform lists headaches that wake someone at night, that are there on waking, that keep getting worse, or that are set off by coughing, sneezing or bending as reasons for an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111.
Taking painkillers regularly can itself cause daily headaches, a problem called medication overuse headache.

body.heading: What are the common types of headache?
body.body:
NHS inform describes tension-type headache as the most common kind. The NHS says tension headaches are not a sign of an underlying condition, and common triggers include stress, sleep problems and caffeine.

Migraine usually causes a moderate or severe throbbing pain, often on one side of the head. Other migraine symptoms include feeling sick and sensitivity to light and sound. Some people also get an aura, such as seeing zigzag lines or flashing lights. NHS inform says migraine affects around 1 in 5 women and 1 in 15 men. Cluster headaches are rare, and each attack is intensely painful, affects one side of the head and can happen several times a day.

body.heading: Can painkillers cause headaches?
body.body: Taking painkillers regularly can itself cause daily headaches, a problem called medication overuse headache. NHS inform says it usually affects people who already have tension-type headaches or migraines. Stopping the overused medicine usually helps, although the pain can get worse for a few days first. People who get headaches often and take painkillers regularly are advised to speak to a GP.

body.heading: Which headaches need a 999 call?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that comes on suddenly and is extremely painful, or one that follows a serious head injury. Other reasons to call 999 include weakness on one side, slurred speech, trouble speaking or remembering, loss of vision, drowsiness, confusion, or a high temperature with a stiff neck or a rash that could mean meningitis.

body.heading: Which headaches need an urgent GP visit?
body.body: NHS inform lists headaches that wake someone at night, that are there on waking, that keep getting worse, or that are set off by coughing, sneezing or bending as reasons for an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111. A new headache in a person over 50, with a sore scalp or jaw pain when chewing, can signal inflamed arteries and also needs urgent attention. Headaches with vision changes, or with vomiting plus dizziness or weakness, also call for urgent review. An NHS formulary guideline describes giant cell arteritis, also called temporal arteritis, as a medical emergency that needs prompt assessment and immediate steroid treatment to prevent permanent loss of vision. An NHS trust page lists tiredness, loss of appetite, weight loss, fever and headache, with tenderness over the temples, jaw or tongue pain when eating, and blurred vision, as its symptoms.

body.heading: How is migraine treated?
body.body: NHS pages describe triptans as a painkiller designed for migraine, which works by reversing the widening of blood vessels that is believed to be part of the migraine process. If ordinary painkillers do not relieve migraine symptoms, the NHS advises making a GP appointment. Anti-sickness medicines can help during a migraine even without nausea, and the NHS says they work better when taken as soon as symptoms begin. An NHS-hosted leaflet advises against strong opioid painkillers such as codeine, tramadol and morphine for migraine because of the high risk of rebound headache. The NHS lists common migraine triggers as stress, tiredness, lack of sleep, dehydration, missing meals, regular alcohol or caffeine, and foods such as cheese or chocolate, and suggests keeping a record to spot personal triggers.

body.heading: When is a routine GP visit sensible, and what might the GP do?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP for tension headaches that happen several times a week, are severe, or do not respond to painkillers and relaxation. These can be signs of a different type of headache, such as migraine or cluster headache. A GP may suggest keeping a headache diary that records how often the headaches happen and how long they last. There is no specific test for migraine, so the GP looks for a pattern of recurring headaches with the typical symptoms. Simple painkillers, rest and fluids are the first step for most headaches. If painkillers and exercise do not help, a person may be referred to a specialist, and a medicine called amitriptyline may be offered to help prevent tension headaches.

shortness-of-breath-causes-and-next-step.name: Shortness of breath: causes and next steps
shortness-of-breath-causes-and-next-step.summary: Breathlessness has many causes, from asthma and anxiety to heart and lung disease, and severe difficulty breathing needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: NHS inform lists asthma attacks, pneumonia and heart failure among the likely causes of sudden breathlessness.
Sudden breathlessness could be an asthma attack, in which the airways narrow and make extra sticky mucus, causing wheeze and cough.
NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe difficulty breathing, such as being unable to speak without pausing for breath.
The NHS advises contacting NHS 111 or the GP urgently for worsening breathlessness, feeling sick, coughing up blood, or pain or swelling in one leg.

body.heading: Why do people get short of breath?
body.body:
NHS inform lists asthma attacks, pneumonia and heart failure among the likely causes of sudden breathlessness. Less common sudden causes include a severe allergic reaction, a collapsed lung and a blood clot in the lung. A collapsed lung, or pneumothorax, is a partial collapse caused by a small tear in the lung surface, and a pulmonary embolism is a blockage in one of the blood vessels in the lung.

Breathlessness that lasts a long time is commonly linked to obesity, being unfit, poorly controlled asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), anaemia, heart failure and heart rhythm problems. In heart failure, fluid builds up in the lungs and makes breathing harder. A panic attack or anxiety can make a person breathe fast or deeply, which is called hyperventilating.

body.heading: What do asthma, COPD, heart failure and a lung clot look like?
body.body: Sudden breathlessness could be an asthma attack, in which the airways narrow and make extra sticky mucus, causing wheeze and cough. Typical COPD symptoms include increasing breathlessness when active, a persistent cough with phlegm and frequent chest infections. The NHS lists breathlessness as the most common symptom of heart failure; it may happen after activity or at rest, may be worse when lying down, and may wake a person at night. It lists tiredness, swollen ankles and legs, and feeling lightheaded or fainting as other heart failure symptoms. An NHS trust leaflet says the most common symptom of a pulmonary embolism is breathlessness, with other symptoms including chest pain that is worse on breathing or coughing, cough, fever and coughing up blood.

body.heading: When is breathlessness an emergency?
body.body: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe difficulty breathing, such as being unable to speak without pausing for breath. Chest tightness, or pain that spreads to the arms, back, neck or jaw, is also a reason to call 999. A GP practice page adds sudden confusion, or lips or skin turning pale, blue or grey, to the signs that need an emergency response. NHS 111 Wales advises that a person should not drive themselves to A&E but should ask someone to take them or call an ambulance.

body.heading: When should breathlessness be seen urgently or soon?
body.body: The NHS advises contacting NHS 111 or the GP urgently for worsening breathlessness, feeling sick, coughing up blood, or pain or swelling in one leg. NHS inform says breathlessness that starts suddenly should be seen urgently by a GP because it may point to a problem with the airways or heart. For breathlessness that comes on slowly, NHS inform advises seeing a GP if it has lasted more than a month, gets worse with activity or lying down, or comes with swollen ankles.

body.heading: What does the GP ask about and test?
body.body: A GP will usually ask when the breathlessness started, what brings it on and whether lying down makes it worse. An NHS England pathway for persistent breathlessness lists blood tests, an ECG, a chest X-ray and spirometry among the first tests. Spirometry is a breathing test that measures how much air a person can blow out and how fast. If the cause is still unclear, the same pathway lists further tests such as a CT scan of the chest, an echocardiogram and ambulatory ECG monitoring.

body.heading: How is breathlessness treated?
body.body: Treatment depends on the cause. For COPD, treatment usually involves relieving symptoms with medicines such as inhalers, and pulmonary rehabilitation may help. Heart failure is managed with lifestyle changes and medicines or surgery. A blood clot in the lung can be treated with anticoagulants, which are drugs that thin the blood. One NHS leaflet describes relaxed breathing and pursed-lip breathing as techniques that can help a person regain control of their breathing.

stomach-ache-causes-by-area-and-warning-.name: Stomach ache: causes by area and warning signs
stomach-ache-causes-by-area-and-warning-.summary: Where a stomach ache sits helps point to causes such as appendicitis, gallstones or IBS, and sudden severe pain needs 999 or A&E.
keyPoints: The NHS lists trapped wind, indigestion, constipation and a stomach bug or food poisoning as common everyday causes of stomach ache.
The NHS stomach ache page links pain in the lower right side of the tummy with appendicitis.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the ache suddenly gets much worse, if the person is pregnant, if there is blood in the poo, or if diarrhoea or vomiting has lasted several days.

body.heading: What usually causes a stomach ache?
body.body: The NHS lists trapped wind, indigestion, constipation and a stomach bug or food poisoning as common everyday causes of stomach ache. Period pain and endometriosis are listed as causes of pain in the lower tummy in women.

body.heading: Does the area of the pain point to a cause?
body.body:
The NHS stomach ache page links pain in the lower right side of the tummy with appendicitis. It links severe pain that lasts up to 8 hours in the centre of the tummy, or just under the ribs on the right, with gallstones. It links ongoing cramps, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

NHS inform describes appendicitis as painful swelling of the appendix, and says the pain of IBS is often relieved by going to the toilet. Stomach ulcer pain is usually in the upper tummy, may feel burning and is often worse at night. Gastritis can cause pain, indigestion and feeling sick. Gastritis is inflammation of the lining of the stomach. Acute pancreatitis causes severe pain that develops suddenly in the centre of the tummy, and the NHS says its most common causes are gallstones and drinking a lot of alcohol.

body.heading: What do appendicitis, gallstones and diverticular disease look like?
body.body: Appendicitis is when the appendix becomes inflamed; it usually causes pain in the lower right side of the tummy and is sometimes accompanied by nausea and loss of appetite. An NHS 111 Wales page says appendicitis needs urgent treatment in hospital. A hospital trust page says gallstones do not always cause symptoms, but can lead to pain after eating, inflammation of the gallbladder, pancreatitis or jaundice. The NHS says diverticular disease causes pain in the lower left side of the tummy that often gets worse after eating and eases after passing wind or stool, with constipation, diarrhoea, bloating or blood in the stool. It adds that the symptoms are similar to those of other conditions such as IBS. For diverticular disease the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for blood in the stool, worsening or persistent tummy pain, or a fever, and says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass stool or wind, or signs of sepsis.

body.heading: When is stomach pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe. Other reasons are vomiting blood or vomit that looks green or like ground coffee, a lot of blood from the bottom or black, sticky poo, being unable to pee at all, being unable to poo or fart at all, a rash that does not fade when pressed, or struggling to breathe. NHS inform adds chest pain, and pain that hurts when the stomach is touched, to the reasons to call 999. For acute pancreatitis, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain spreads to the back, or if there is a fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing.

body.heading: When should it be checked the same day or by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the ache suddenly gets much worse, if the person is pregnant, if there is blood in the poo, or if diarrhoea or vomiting has lasted several days. It advises a GP appointment for pain, bloating or indigestion that does not go away or keeps coming back, for a lump in the tummy, or for losing weight without trying.

body.heading: What might a GP do?
body.body: Treatment depends on the cause. For gastritis, a GP might arrange a breath test for Helicobacter pylori bacteria, a stool test or a blood test. Stomach ulcers may be treated with antibiotics for a Helicobacter pylori infection or with medicines that reduce stomach acid, such as proton pump inhibitors. Gastroenteritis often has no specific treatment, and the illness has to run its course.

references.title: NHS inform: Stomach ache and abdominal pain

back-pain-what-helps-and-when-to-get-hel.name: Back pain: what helps and when to get help
back-pain-what-helps-and-when-to-get-hel.summary: Most back pain settles with time and staying active helps, but numbness around the genitals or loss of bladder or bowel control needs A&E.
keyPoints: NHS sources say that staying active is part of treatment and that most back pain settles with time.
NICE guideline NG59 on low back pain and sciatica in people over 16 recommends advice and information that help people manage their own pain, and staying active.
NHS sources suggest asking a GP or an NHS physiotherapist for advice if back symptoms are still getting in the way of normal activities after about 6 weeks.
Cauda equina syndrome is a rare but serious condition that needs emergency treatment.

body.heading: What causes back pain?
body.body: An NHS back pain page says a strain is a common cause and that serious causes such as a fracture, cancer or infection are very rare. The NHS says a slipped disc is the most common cause of sciatica, and the likelihood rises with age. Other causes of sciatica include spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis and a back injury. Sciatica is pain that spreads from the lower back down the leg because the sciatic nerve is irritated.

body.heading: What helps back pain?
body.body: NHS sources say that staying active is part of treatment and that most back pain settles with time. NHS inform describes keeping active as the single best thing a person can do for their back. In most cases, back pain gets better after a few weeks. NHS trust leaflets suggest gentle movements, walking, swimming or cycling, and say that any type of exercise can be worthwhile if it is something the person enjoys. They generally suggest a cold pack in the first few days and heat afterwards, with a cloth between the pack and the skin. Prolonged bed rest can leave the back stiff and the muscles weak, and a physiotherapist can design a personal exercise plan. Bed rest during the day is no longer recommended, because people who stay active tend to get better more quickly. The NHS sciatica page suggests staying active, doing regular exercises and asking a pharmacist about painkillers, and notes that paracetamol is unlikely to help sciatica. The NHS back pain page says paracetamol on its own is not recommended for back pain and that anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen may not suit everyone.

body.heading: What does NICE recommend for low back pain?
body.body: NICE guideline NG59 on low back pain and sciatica in people over 16 recommends advice and information that help people manage their own pain, and staying active. It recommends manual therapy only as part of a package of care that includes exercise. It does not recommend belts or corsets, foot orthotics, traction, or TENS and interferential therapy.

body.heading: When should back pain be seen by a GP or physiotherapist?
body.body: NHS sources suggest asking a GP or an NHS physiotherapist for advice if back symptoms are still getting in the way of normal activities after about 6 weeks. NHS 111 Wales says physiotherapy is free on the NHS, though waiting times can be long, and that in some areas people can refer themselves without seeing a GP. Sciatica usually improves within weeks to months, though it can last longer and may come back.

body.heading: What are the emergency signs?
body.body: Cauda equina syndrome is a rare but serious condition that needs emergency treatment. NHS sources list its warning signs as loss of bladder or bowel control or feeling, being unable to pass urine, numbness around the genitals or back passage, and worsening weakness or pain in both legs. They say that a person who develops these signs after back pain should go to the nearest A&E department.

references.title: NICE NG59: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s

knee-pain-causes-self-care-and-when-to-a.name: Knee pain: causes and when to get help
knee-pain-causes-self-care-and-when-to-a.summary: Most knee pain settles with gentle activity, and a GP visit is advised if it does not improve, while a badly swollen or hot, red knee needs NHS 111.
keyPoints: The NHS knee pain page lists sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, damage to the meniscus or cartilage, a dislocated kneecap, osteoarthritis, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter disease.
The NHS describes reducing weight on the knee, using a cold pack wrapped in a tea towel for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours, and taking paracetamol or ibuprofen for the pain.
The NHS advises a GP visit if knee pain does not improve within a few weeks.
The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.

body.heading: What causes knee pain?
body.body: The NHS knee pain page lists sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, damage to the meniscus or cartilage, a dislocated kneecap, osteoarthritis, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter disease. Overuse or injury often causes sudden knee pain. An NHS trust leaflet describes osteoarthritis as cartilage gradually worn away with age or after injury, mainly at the points of greatest pressure. It can cause pain, stiffness, loss of movement, swelling and deformity. NHS inform says the exact cause of knee osteoarthritis is unclear, and risk factors include ageing, a previous knee injury, being overweight and family history. Imaging and symptoms do not always match, because many people with signs of osteoarthritis on an X-ray have very mild symptoms or none. NHS sources say that strengthening the thigh muscles is commonly recommended for knee osteoarthritis, and that exercise does not speed up the arthritis.

body.heading: What can ease it at home?
body.body: The NHS describes reducing weight on the knee, using a cold pack wrapped in a tea towel for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours, and taking paracetamol or ibuprofen for the pain. Staying gently active is also advised. An NHS trust says keeping active and gradually returning to usual activities helps recovery.

body.heading: When should knee pain be seen by a GP or physiotherapist?
body.body: The NHS advises a GP visit if knee pain does not improve within a few weeks. The NHS says people may be able to refer themselves to community musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy services without seeing a GP. An NHS trust leaflet describes physiotherapy as the mainstay of treatment for pain at the front of the knee. Management of knee osteoarthritis includes exercise programmes, pain relief and footwear advice, according to an NHS trust. A guide from another trust mentions an MRI scan if a ligament or meniscus tear could be the cause.

body.heading: Which signs need urgent help?
body.body: The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection. An NHS trust A&E leaflet advises attending A&E after a high-impact injury with immediate swelling, a pop, severe pain or inability to put weight on the leg, or for a knee or leg that looks deformed.

joint-pain-causes-and-when-to-see-a-gp.name: Joint pain: causes and when to see a GP
joint-pain-causes-and-when-to-see-a-gp.summary: Joint pain is often osteoarthritis, injury or gout, and a sudden hot, swollen joint with fever needs an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.
keyPoints: The NHS joint pain page links pain after intense exercise to a sprain or strain.
The NHS says to rest the joint but not stop moving it altogether, and that a pharmacist or GP can advise about painkillers.
The NHS suggests a GP appointment if joint pain stops normal activities or affects sleep, keeps getting worse or coming back, or has not improved after 2 weeks of treating it at home.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for severe pain and swelling in one joint that started suddenly.

body.heading: What causes joint pain?
body.body: The NHS joint pain page links pain after intense exercise to a sprain or strain. It links pain that is worse with walking, usually in people over 45, with osteoarthritis. NHS 111 Wales describes osteoarthritis as the most common type of arthritis in the UK. Gout is a form of arthritis in which small crystals form inside and around the joints. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the lining of the joints, usually in the hands, feet and wrists, with pain that is typically worse in the mornings or after inactivity. The NHS says rheumatoid arthritis is usually first felt in the small joints of the hands and feet. The NHS arthritis overview says gout often affects the big toe joint, which can become painful, swollen and hot. Psoriatic arthritis is a long-term condition that causes joint pain, swelling and stiffness, and the NHS says it affects about 1 in 4 people who have the skin condition psoriasis.

body.heading: What can ease joint pain at home?
body.body: The NHS says to rest the joint but not stop moving it altogether, and that a pharmacist or GP can advise about painkillers. Losing weight and eating a balanced diet also help. For osteoarthritis the NHS says treatment focuses on exercise, weight management, pain relief and supportive measures such as hot or cold packs. NHS 111 Wales says osteoarthritis has no cure but does not necessarily get worse over time.

body.heading: When is a GP appointment sensible?
body.body: The NHS suggests a GP appointment if joint pain stops normal activities or affects sleep, keeps getting worse or coming back, or has not improved after 2 weeks of treating it at home. It also lists joints that stay stiff for more than 30 minutes after waking. For gout, the NHS advises seeing a GP for a first episode, or when the usual treatments are not helping.

body.heading: Which joint pain needs urgent help?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for severe pain and swelling in one joint that started suddenly. A warm, swollen joint that is hard to move, with a high temperature or feeling hot and shivery, may mean a joint infection called septic arthritis.

body.heading: How is the cause found?
body.body: A GP examines the joints for swelling, checks how easily they move and asks about symptoms. Blood tests such as ESR, CRP and a full blood count may be used, and X-rays or MRI scans may show inflammation and damage. There is no single definitive test for rheumatoid arthritis, so diagnosis can be difficult. If rheumatoid arthritis is suspected, the GP usually refers the person to a rheumatologist. A rheumatologist is a doctor who specialises in conditions of the joints and immune system.

feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults.name: Feeling sick and vomiting in adults
feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults.summary: Nausea and vomiting in adults usually pass within a day or two, but vomiting blood needs A&E and being sick for more than 2 days needs NHS 111.
keyPoints: The NHS says feeling sick is common and usually goes away on its own.
NHS inform lists confusion, a fast heartbeat, sunken eyes and passing little or no urine as warning signs of dehydration.
The NHS says to go to A&E for vomit that contains blood or looks like ground coffee, or for green vomit.

NHS inform advises calling NHS 111 for a person who keeps being sick and cannot keep fluids down, has been vomiting for more than 2 days, has lost a lot of weight since becoming ill, has a fever, or has bloody diarrhoea.

body.heading: What causes nausea and vomiting?
body.body: The NHS says feeling sick is common and usually goes away on its own. Diarrhoea or vomiting can point to norovirus or food poisoning, and a headache with a high temperature can suggest an infection such as flu. Other causes include morning sickness in pregnancy, motion sickness, anxiety, alcohol, medicines and recent surgery. NHS inform calls gastroenteritis one of the most common causes of vomiting in adults, and also lists migraine, labyrinthitis, appendicitis and medicines such as antibiotics and opioid painkillers. NHS trust leaflets say norovirus symptoms usually clear within a few days, and that apart from letting the illness run its course there is no specific treatment. The main advice in those leaflets is to drink fluids to prevent dehydration, and antibiotics do not work because norovirus is a virus.

body.heading: What can help at home?
body.body: The NHS describes getting fresh air, sipping cold drinks, trying ginger or peppermint tea, and eating smaller, more frequent meals. It also lists hot, fried or greasy food, eating too quickly and lying down soon after eating as things to avoid. NHS inform advises resting at home and taking small sips of water or squash often so that dehydration does not develop.

body.heading: What are the signs of dehydration?
body.body: NHS inform lists confusion, a fast heartbeat, sunken eyes and passing little or no urine as warning signs of dehydration. NHS inform advises people with diabetes who have been vomiting a lot to call NHS 111, especially if they take insulin, because vomiting can affect blood sugar levels.

body.heading: Which symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: The NHS says to go to A&E for vomit that contains blood or looks like ground coffee, or for green vomit. NHS inform advises calling NHS 111 for a person who keeps being sick and cannot keep fluids down, has been vomiting for more than 2 days, has lost a lot of weight since becoming ill, has a fever, or has bloody diarrhoea. The NHS says to call 999 if sudden sickness comes with tight or heavy chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, back, neck or jaw, or shortness of breath, because these could be signs of a heart attack.

body.heading: When should a GP be involved?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if the sickness has not improved after a few days or keeps coming back, and calling NHS 111 for advice if a GP cannot be seen. The GP can look for the cause and may prescribe anti-sickness medicine. The NHS says a pregnant person who is being sick often and cannot keep food down should tell their midwife or doctor, or contact the hospital, as soon as possible.

references.title: www.uhs.nhs.uk: Gastroenteritis caused by norovirus and other viruses patient information.pdf

persistent-cough-causes-tests-and-when-t.name: A cough that will not go: causes and tests
persistent-cough-causes-tests-and-when-t.summary: A cough that has lasted more than 3 weeks should be checked by a GP, and coughing up blood or trouble breathing needs urgent help.
keyPoints: The NHS advises seeing a GP if a cough has lasted more than 3 weeks, if weight is being lost for no reason, or if the immune system is weakened.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough with chest pain or a feeling of being very unwell.
A GP will ask how long the cough has lasted and about other symptoms, and may examine the chest.
The NHS says most coughs can be managed at home with rest and fluids, and a pharmacist can advise on cough medicines.

body.heading: What causes a cough that lasts?
body.body: The NHS says most coughs are caused by a cold or flu. The NHS cough page lists smoking, heartburn (acid reflux), allergies and infections such as bronchitis as causes. Persistent coughs can also come from asthma, bronchiectasis, and postnasal drip from hay fever or other nose problems. ACE inhibitors, a type of blood pressure medicine, can cause a long-lasting cough in some people. For many people the cause of a long-lasting cough is never identified. The NHS says bronchitis usually clears up without treatment in around 3 weeks, and advises seeing a GP if symptoms last longer. A chest infection usually gets better on its own in about 7 to 10 days, although the cough and mucus can last up to 3 weeks. Antibiotics are generally not used for viral chest infections such as flu or viral bronchitis.

body.heading: What can help at home?
body.body: The NHS says most coughs can be managed at home with rest and fluids, and a pharmacist can advise on cough medicines. The NHS says there is little evidence on whether over-the-counter cough medicines relieve symptoms. An NHS self-care leaflet says stopping or cutting down smoking can help a cough.

body.heading: When should a cough be seen by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if a cough has lasted more than 3 weeks, if weight is being lost for no reason, or if the immune system is weakened. An NHS cancer alliance says a cough is rarely a sign of something serious such as lung cancer, but encourages people with a cough lasting three weeks or more to contact their GP practice so that any serious cause is found early. It lists other lung cancer symptoms as coughing up blood, pain when breathing or coughing, persistent breathlessness and persistent tiredness.

body.heading: When is a cough urgent?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough with chest pain or a feeling of being very unwell. Coughing up blood and difficulty breathing also need prompt attention, and for trouble breathing the NHS says to call 999. For people with bronchiectasis, the NHS says to call 999 if more than a few streaks of blood are coughed up.

body.heading: What does the GP do?
body.body: A GP will ask how long the cough has lasted and about other symptoms, and may examine the chest. Tests can include a lung function test, a chest X-ray, and a sample of any mucus. Treatment depends on the cause, antibiotics are not normally prescribed for coughs, and a referral to a chest specialist is occasionally needed.

sore-throat-causes-treatment-and-when-to.name: Sore throat: causes, treatment, when to act
sore-throat-causes-treatment-and-when-to.summary: Most sore throats are caused by viruses and clear up on their own, but struggling to breathe or swallow needs 999 or A&E.
keyPoints: The NHS says most sore throats are caused by viruses such as colds or flu, and bacteria are a less common cause.
A sore throat usually clears up on its own and often lasts about a week.
NICE says most people with a sore throat will not need an antibiotic.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for struggling to breathe, being unable to swallow even with pain relief, or drooling or spitting out saliva because swallowing is too painful.

body.heading: What causes a sore throat?
body.body: The NHS says most sore throats are caused by viruses such as colds or flu, and bacteria are a less common cause. Laryngitis, tonsillitis, strep throat and glandular fever can also cause a sore throat, and so can smoking. NICE says that in older children and adults, pus on the tonsils, painful glands in the neck and a fever without a cough point more towards a bacterial infection.

body.heading: How long does it last, and what helps?
body.body: A sore throat usually clears up on its own and often lasts about a week. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can help with pain and fever, although not everyone can take ibuprofen safely, so a pharmacist can advise. Drinking fluids and resting are also advised.

body.heading: Are antibiotics needed?
body.body: NICE says most people with a sore throat will not need an antibiotic. The NHS says antibiotics are prescribed only if the GP thinks a bacterial infection is likely.

body.heading: What are tonsillitis, glandular fever and quinsy?
body.body: Tonsillitis commonly causes a sore throat, trouble swallowing, fever, earache and tender swollen glands in the neck. A GP can usually diagnose tonsillitis from the symptoms and a look at the throat, and may arrange a swab or a glandular fever blood test if symptoms are severe or persistent. Glandular fever can cause a high temperature, swollen glands, a sore throat, rash, headache and tiredness, and the NHS says it is most common in people aged 15 to 24. Antibiotics do not work for glandular fever because it is caused by a virus. Quinsy is a collection of pus between the tonsil and the wall of the throat, and is a rare complication of tonsillitis.

body.heading: When should a GP be seen?
body.body: Sources agree on seeking advice from a GP if the sore throat has not improved after a week, if there is a high temperature or the person feels hot and shivery, or if the immune system is weakened or a medicine could be causing the sore throat. A sore throat that does not get better within 10 to 14 days, or that gets worse rather than better, may suggest glandular fever.

body.heading: When is a sore throat an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for struggling to breathe, being unable to swallow even with pain relief, or drooling or spitting out saliva because swallowing is too painful. Other reasons are a high-pitched noise when breathing in, a sore throat that is severe and getting worse quickly, swelling inside the mouth or throat, or trouble speaking. NHS 111 Wales advises that a person should not drive themselves to A&E but should ask someone to drive them or call 999.
